strengths: The architecture is simple and mathematically transparent: excluding feature j from its correction network and anchoring the correction at zero yields the exact identity MEM_j = beta_j after standardization.

The paper identifies a useful modeling goal—combining context-dependent nonlinear interactions with a globally accessible linear component—and the shared network with positional encodings avoids requiring one network per feature.

The variable-elimination perspective is potentially useful, and the paper includes regression and classification formulations, synthetic studies, several real tabular datasets, competitive baselines, and an ablation of masking and positional encoding.
The manuscript is generally clear, and the synthetic examples visually demonstrate recovery of coefficients, sparsity patterns, and selected nonlinearities under favorable data-generating processes.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is overstated. The per-instance correction h_j(x) is not the local marginal effect of feature j under the paper's own definition: changing x_j also changes every other correction g_i(x_-i) that consumes x_j, producing the cross-terms shown in Section 3.2. Thus h_j alone does not explain the local effect of feature j, yet the paper repeatedly presents these corrections as local explanations and does not evaluate the complete marginal effects.

MEM is a derivative at the single all-features-at-their-means point, not a population-level average effect. Calling beta_j an additive population-level contribution is especially questionable with interactions, correlated features, or little data support near the joint mean. No stability, identifiability, or uncertainty analysis is provided for these coefficients.

The optimization presentation has important gaps and inconsistencies. The equality-constrained adaptive-ridge problem is replaced by a penalized objective without clearly establishing the parameter correspondence; Algorithm 1 does not enforce c_i >= 0 or the stated norm constraint and uses lambda||gamma|| where the derivation uses lambda||gamma||^2. The intercept also disappears from the matrix derivation. For logistic regression, an IRLS iterate depending on the previous coefficient estimate is treated as if it were a closed-form elimination; the required inner convergence or implicit differentiation procedure is not specified.

The synthetic generators are constructed almost exactly in NIMO's assumed functional form, so the large advantage mainly demonstrates well-specified-model recovery. Results appear to be single point estimates without repeated datasets, uncertainty, or sensitivity analysis, and there is no quantitative evaluation of the claimed per-instance explanation accuracy.

The real-data evidence is limited to three old tabular regression datasets. Interpretability is not validated against ground truth or domain knowledge; agreement between NIMO's MEM ranking and SHAP applied to NIMO is not evidence of correctness. Claims of significant predictive improvements are made without statistical tests, while exact numerical means and variances are not reported.

Relevant alternatives are insufficiently covered, including varying-coefficient models, self-explaining neural networks, interaction-aware additive models such as EBM/GA2M or GAMI-Net, and the cited Contextual Lasso. The paper's assertion that marginal effects of other nonlinear models are merely arbitrary is also unsupported.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a top-tier submission: network depths and widths, batch size, epochs and stopping rules, penalty grids, noise-injection magnitude, preprocessing details, and SHAP configuration are missing, and no code is supplied. The repetition protocol is internally inconsistent: the main text reports 9/9/5 seeds, whereas the appendix states five runs for every real dataset.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the main local- and global-interpretability claims are not supported at the strength stated, and the optimization and empirical validation require substantial clarification and expansion.

strengths: The manuscript presents a simple, understandable hybrid architecture, and the masking constraint yields the exact mathematical property that the derivative at the standardized origin equals the corresponding coefficient. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/7796a2195dc24429960f0ec86bbb62b4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Parameter elimination is a potentially useful way to combine closed-form linear updates with neural optimization, while the adaptive-ridge formulation offers a natural route to coefficient sparsity.
The synthetic experiments cover regression, classification, dimensionality, nonlinear interactions, and irrelevant features; the masking and positional-encoding ablations are directionally useful.
The paper is generally well organized, and the appendix provides derivations, data-generating processes, and some implementation information.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is overstated. The coefficient beta_j is the derivative at one specific point—the standardized origin—not a population-level or global additive effect. MEM is not an average marginal effect, the mean may be outside the data support, and the quantity can be unstable under correlated features or distribution shift. Showing that NIMO and Lasso produce different coefficients on real data does not establish that NIMO's coefficients are more meaningful.

The claimed local explanations are not justified. The displayed correction beta_j(1+g_j(x_-j)) is not the marginal effect of feature j: as the paper's own equation shows, the derivative also contains cross-derivative terms from every other component. Moreover, each correction is produced by an opaque multivariate neural network. No user study, faithfulness criterion, stability analysis, or comparison against ground-truth local effects supports calling these outputs intelligible explanations.

The synthetic generators are constructed to match NIMO's functional form, giving the proposed method a substantial structural advantage. The real-data experiments have no interpretability ground truth, and agreement with SHAP applied to the same fitted model is not independent validation. Consequently, the experiments do not support the main interpretability claims.

The empirical scope is too limited for a top-tier contribution: only three old tabular regression datasets are used, including the deprecated and ethically problematic Boston Housing dataset. Important predictive and interpretable baselines—such as boosted trees, EBM/GA2M, and interaction-aware additive models—are absent. The method is therefore not shown to offer a competitive accuracy–interpretability trade-off against standard strong alternatives.

Statistical reporting is inadequate and internally inconsistent. The main text reports 9 seeds for Diabetes and Boston and 5 for Superconductivity, whereas Appendix D.4 states 5 runs for every dataset. Real-data results are shown mainly as plots without numerical summaries or significance tests, while synthetic tables provide no uncertainty and appear to rely on a single split. Baseline tuning budgets are also insufficiently specified.

The optimization section contains consequential inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 uses an unsquared norm for the gamma penalty whereas the derivation uses a squared norm; the sub-l1 section repeats this discrepancy; positivity of c is required but not enforced by the stated gradient update; and the relationship between the constrained formulation and the penalized Lagrangian implementation is not rigorously explained. These issues prevent the claimed Lasso equivalence from being cleanly connected to the actual algorithm.

Efficiency and scalability claims are unsupported. Training requires evaluating masked inputs across features and solving a feature-dimensional linear system at every update, yet no runtime, memory, convergence, or scaling comparison is reported; the largest experiment has only 81 features. Reproducibility is further limited by missing architecture details, candidate hyperparameter grids, training schedules, and an implementation of NIMO.

The sparsity evidence is largely qualitative heatmaps. There are no support-recovery metrics, stability measurements across seeds, sensitivity analyses for the group penalty and noise injection, or evidence that first-layer weight sparsity reliably identifies interactions in a multilayer network. Overall, the idea is plausible, but the technical presentation and evaluation do not substantiate the paper's strongest claims.

MEM should not be conflated with an average marginal effect, and the estimate can be an unstable extrapolation when the joint feature mean lies outside the data manifold, particularly with correlated features.

The real-data evaluation is too limited for a top-tier claim: it uses only three conventional datasets, including the deprecated Boston Housing dataset, and omits strong predictive and interpretable tabular baselines such as gradient-boosted trees, Explainable Boosting Machines, and interaction-aware GAMs. No statistical tests or numerical result tables are supplied.

The experiments do not validate the explanations against known real-world effects or compare local marginal effects with appropriate explanation methods. Agreement between NIMO's MEM ranking and SHAP applied to the same model is not independent evidence of correctness, especially because SHAP importance and a signed derivative at the mean measure different quantities.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: there is no code release, and essential architecture, training-duration, candidate-grid, noise-injection, and coefficient-thresholding details are missing. strengths: The core architecture is simple and intuitively motivated: masking feature j from its correction network guarantees that the coefficient beta_j equals the model derivative at the standardized mean.

The paper clearly distinguishes the model’s global coefficients from its context-dependent corrections, acknowledges its inability to represent self-nonlinearities, and demonstrates that limitation empirically.

The evaluation includes regression and classification, synthetic coefficient-recovery experiments, several real datasets, feature-masking and sparsity ablations, and comparisons with LassoNet, NAM, and IMN.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the synthetic experiments show promising prediction and support-recovery behavior when the data-generating process matches NIMO’s assumed form.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is overstated. Beta_j is a derivative at the single point x=0, not generally a population-level additive effect. The nonlinear cross-derivative terms vanish there only because every feature is evaluated at zero. This point can be unrepresentative or off the data manifold, particularly with correlated inputs. Merely calling the remaining network terms 'local corrections' does not make beta an average or population effect.

The treatment of local explanations is internally inconsistent. The paper correctly derives that the marginal effect contains cross terms from other correction networks, but later presents s_j(x)=beta_j(1+g_j(x_-j)) as a local coefficient. This quantity is not the local marginal effect. Its associated contribution is an exact architectural decomposition, but allocation of interactions among features is model-dependent and is not shown to be uniquely or semantically identifiable.

The adaptive-ridge optimization description has serious inconsistencies. The claimed Lasso equivalence requires the constraint sum_j c_j^2=d, whereas the proposed algorithm replaces it with a fixed positive penalty and performs unconstrained gradient updates, without enforcing either the equality or c_j>=0. Moreover, the objective alternates between squared and unsquared norms of gamma, while the stated closed-form ridge solution is valid for the squared penalty. These discrepancies undermine the claimed equivalence and make the implemented objective unclear.

The logistic extension is incomplete: an IRLS update is not a closed-form elimination of gamma as a function of the network parameters unless the inner IRLS problem is solved to convergence, and the optimization/differentiation procedure through those iterations is not specified.

The synthetic evaluation is strongly aligned with the proposed architecture: almost all generating functions are explicitly of NIMO's x_j beta_j[1+g_j(x_-j)] form. Results are generally reported without uncertainty across independently generated datasets, so they provide limited evidence of robust coefficient recovery under misspecification.

The real-data interpretability evidence is weak because no ground-truth effects exist. Agreement with SHAP from the same fitted model is neither independent validation nor evidence that the claimed population interpretation is correct. Differences from Lasso are discussed qualitatively without statistical or domain validation.

Predictive evaluation is insufficiently rigorous for a top-tier claim: the main study contains only three conventional datasets, plots often omit exact values and confidence intervals, and the appendix benchmark reports single bars. Hyperparameter treatment appears asymmetric, with NIMO penalties grid-searched while several competitors retain defaults. Important alternatives such as boosted GAMs/EBMs and strong tree ensembles are absent.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code or artifact link, and essential details such as network dimensions, training duration and stopping rules, complete hyperparameter grids, penalty enforcement, preprocessing, and precise benchmark protocol are missing. The paper also inconsistently states nine/five splits in the main text versus five runs in the appendix.

The novelty appears incremental relative to contextual-coefficient and hybrid linear-neural models: the main new structural constraint anchors a contextual coefficient at the feature mean, while parameter elimination and adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence are established techniques. Given the conceptual overclaim, optimization ambiguities, and limited validation, the work is not yet competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The core architecture is simple and understandable: it augments a sparse linear model with context-dependent neural corrections while masking each feature from its own correction network.
For standardized inputs, the construction g_j(0)=0 does mathematically ensure that each coefficient beta_j equals the marginal derivative at the all-feature mean.

The paper includes synthetic recovery experiments, regression and classification variants, feature-masking and sparsity ablations, an explicit failure case involving self-nonlinearity, and additional benchmark results in the appendix.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the figures communicate the proposed architecture and experimental findings clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2f3adaa3cdff45659a6ae909ac893497/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is substantially overstated. A derivative at the single standardized point x=0 is not generally a population-level contribution or global feature effect. It can be unrepresentative or outside the data manifold, especially with correlated inputs. The architecture guarantees the algebraic identity MEM_j=beta_j, but not that beta_j is stable, statistically identifiable from the observed support, or globally meaningful.

The purported local explanations s_j(x) and c_j(x) are not marginal effects: the paper's own derivative formula contains cross-feature terms that these quantities omit. They are one additive allocation of the prediction, and interactions such as x_1x_2 can be assigned to multiple component networks without changing the predictor. This non-uniqueness is not analyzed, so faithfulness of the prediction decomposition does not establish interpretability of the individual components.

The evaluation is heavily favorable to the proposed inductive bias. The principal synthetic targets are generated almost exactly in NIMO's functional form, making coefficient and interaction recovery expected. Robustness in a low-data regime is claimed from a single training size rather than a sample-size study, and the synthetic tables lack uncertainty over repeated draws.

The real-data evidence is insufficient for the claimed accuracy-interpretability trade-off. The main evaluation contains only three conventional regression datasets, two of them very small; the additional PMLB study reports only a bar chart without numerical tables, uncertainty, significance tests, or detailed dataset-selection justification. One benchmark requires manually chosen polynomial expansion.

Important baselines are absent, including strong tabular predictors and interpretable interaction models such as gradient-boosted trees, Explainable Boosting Machines, and NODE-GAM. The closely related contextual/varying-coefficient literature is also inadequately positioned. Consequently, neither predictive competitiveness nor novelty is convincingly established.

The comparison protocol is not sufficiently controlled. Baselines use different implementations, defaults, architectures, regularizers, and selection procedures, accompanied by the non-reproducible statement that the authors 'tried our best.' The main text reports nine splits for Diabetes and Boston and five for Superconductivity, whereas the appendix states five runs for all datasets.

The claimed efficient optimization is unsupported by runtime, memory, convergence, or scaling experiments. NIMO requires evaluating the shared network once per feature and solving a feature-dimensional linear system during training, which may be expensive. The adaptive-ridge/Lasso presentation also conflates an equality constraint with a penalized objective, treats a Lagrange multiplier as a tuned penalty, and does not provide a rigorous convergence argument, particularly for the IRLS extension.

Several empirical interpretations are unjustified. Agreement with SHAP is shown visually without quantitative fidelity metrics or appropriate explanation baselines. The proposed 'degree of nonlinearity,' mean |1+g_j|, measures correction magnitude rather than nonlinear variation. Differences in feature rankings and the near-zero coefficient of Boston's controversial B feature are given substantive interpretations despite correlation and selection instability.

Reproducibility is weak: exact network dimensions, epoch budgets, stopping rules, candidate hyperparameter grids, normalization details, and complete numerical results are missing, and no code or artifact release is identified.

Overall, the paper contains a plausible modeling idea and useful diagnostic experiments, but the main contribution rests on relabeling a reference-point derivative as global population interpretability. Combined with non-identifiable local allocations, incomplete baselines, and limited evaluation, the evidence is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: NIMO offers a clear and intuitive architecture: contextual neural corrections augment a sparse linear model while the coefficients remain equal to the marginal effects at the standardized mean.

The parameter-elimination formulation is technically interesting and supports both regression and logistic-regression variants, while adaptive-ridge and group penalties encourage complementary forms of sparsity.
The synthetic experiments are well aligned with the proposed model and convincingly demonstrate recovery of coefficients, sparsity patterns, nonlinear interactions, and local contribution terms.

The paper includes useful ablations of masking, positional encoding, and first-layer regularization, and it candidly demonstrates the model's inability to represent self-nonlinearities without basis expansion.
Results on several real datasets and the additional PMLB benchmark suggest competitive predictive performance, while the manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is overstated: a derivative at the single all-mean input is not generally a population-level or global effect. The architectural constraint makes beta equal to MEM, but it does not make that local derivative representative of the data distribution, especially with correlated inputs or an off-manifold mean.

The proposed local coefficient beta_j(1+g_j(x_-j)) is not the marginal effect of feature j; the paper's own derivative contains cross-feature terms from every other correction network. Although the reported local contributions exactly decompose the prediction, their allocation under interactions is not uniquely justified, weakening the claimed intrinsic local interpretability.

The strongest synthetic results use data-generating processes constructed to match NIMO's functional form, use only 100 test points, and generally lack repeated-run uncertainty. This makes the very large performance advantages less persuasive as evidence of broad robustness.

The real-data study omits important tabular and interpretable competitors such as boosted trees, Explainable Boosting Machines, and pairwise GAM methods. The PMLB results are presented only graphically, without numerical tables, uncertainty, or statistical comparisons.

Reproducibility is incomplete: essential architecture and training details, penalty-search grids, stopping criteria, and complete per-dataset hyperparameters are not specified, and no code or artifact link is provided. The main text and appendix also disagree about the number of real-data splits.

The claimed efficiency of parameter elimination is not empirically substantiated. NIMO evaluates a shared network over feature-masked copies and repeatedly solves a feature-dimensional linear system, but provides no runtime, memory, or scaling comparison beyond datasets with at most 81 original features.

The adaptive-ridge presentation is imprecise about how its constrained equivalence to Lasso maps to the penalized training objective, how nonnegativity or normalization of the scaling variables is enforced, and how intercepts are handled in the matrix formulation. These details matter for the claimed sparsity equivalence and implementation.
Overall, the idea is promising and technically plausible, but the interpretability claims and evaluation are not yet sufficiently rigorous for a confident top-tier acceptance.
